summary: Gives implementation requirements and usage guidance for cryptographic algorithms in IPsec ESP and AH. The goal is to keep IPsec interoperable while letting it use up-to-date cryptography. It replaces RFC 7321 and is updated by RFC 9395.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8221 lists which algorithms IPsec ESP and AH implementations must, should, or may support. It moves implementations toward authenticated encryption while allowing a gradual change in required algorithms.

questions: which crypto algorithms for esp and ah
which encryption algorithms must ipsec support
why is manual keying discouraged in ipsec
subtitle: Implementation requirements and guidance for IPsec ESP and AH cryptographic algorithms.

tldr.problem: IPsec implementations need algorithms that are secure enough for current use while retaining interoperability across devices and versions.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assigns implementation requirement levels to encryption, authentication, and compression algorithms, and recommends authenticated encryption where available.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8221 obsoletes RFC 7321 and is updated by RFC 9395, so its requirement levels may have later changes.

today: RFC 8221 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 7321 and is updated by RFC 9395. Consult RFC 9395 for later changes to algorithm levels.

sections.title: Purpose and Audience
sections.content:
Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) and Authentication Header (AH) protect data sent over an IPsec Security Association. RFC 8221 updates the algorithm implementation requirements so implementations can adopt current cryptography and remain interoperable.

The recommendations target implementers, not users configuring their own security policy. The document covers IKEv2 parameters; IKEv1 is outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC tells implementers which algorithms their ESP and AH software should support. It does not tell users which algorithms to select for their own connections.

sections.title: Requirement Levels and Gradual Change
sections.content:
The RFC uses the BCP 14 requirement words and defines SHOULD+, SHOULD-, and MUST-. SHOULD+ is likely to become MUST; SHOULD- may move down to MAY; and MUST- is expected to stop being a MUST in a future document.

Algorithm levels are intended to change gradually so implementations can update while staying interoperable. An IoT label identifies levels intended for interoperability with resource-constrained devices and servers that communicate with them.
sections.plainLanguage: Requirement levels show what an implementation needs to support now and may need to support later. The extra plus and minus forms signal expected future changes.

sections.title: Manual Keys and Authenticated Encryption
sections.content:
The RFC says manual keying SHOULD NOT be used. Without a keying protocol such as IKE, IPsec cannot refresh session keys or reliably manage unique identifiers, nonces, initialization vectors, and counters.

Encryption without authentication MUST NOT be used. ESP can combine both services in an AEAD algorithm, use a separate authentication algorithm with non-AEAD encryption, or combine ESP with AH; the RFC does not recommend the last option because of speed and header overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: Manual keys leave important key-management work to administrators and are discouraged. Encrypted traffic also needs authentication so receivers can detect changes.

sections.title: ESP Encryption Algorithm Levels
sections.content:
ENCR_NULL, ENCR_AES_CBC, and ENCR_AES_GCM_16 are MUST. ENCR_AES_CCM_8 and ENCR_CHACHA20_POLY1305 are SHOULD; ENCR_3DES is SHOULD NOT; and several older or unspecified algorithms are MUST NOT.

The MUST level for AES applies to 128-bit and 256-bit keys; 192-bit keys remain MAY. The RFC explains that ENCR_AES_GCM_16 was raised to MUST to favor authenticated encryption, while ENCR_AES_CBC remains required for interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives each encryption method a support level. It requires implementations to support AES-GCM-16 and AES-CBC, while it discourages or forbids several older choices.

sections.title: Authentication and Compression Levels
sections.content:
AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128 is MUST, AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_96 is MUST-, and AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_512_256 is SHOULD. AUTH_NONE is allowed only with authenticated encryption; otherwise it is MUST NOT. Several older authentication methods are also MUST NOT.

Compression remains optional: DEFLATE, LZS, and LZJH are MAY, while IPCOMP_OUI is MUST NOT. The RFC explains these levels as implementation requirements, not user configuration requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Implementations must support a SHA-2 authentication method and should support another SHA-2 method. Compression remains optional under this RFC.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 7321
sections.content:
RFC 8221 moves the requirements toward authenticated encryption and away from SHA-1 and 3DES. AES-GCM-16 moves to MUST, AES-CCM-8 moves to SHOULD, and 3DES moves to SHOULD NOT.

The RFC also changes the requirement levels for authentication algorithms, including AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_96 moving from MUST to MUST-. These changes replace RFC 7321's earlier guidance.
sections.plainLanguage: This revision raises some newer algorithms and lowers the levels for older ones. RFC 9395 later updates this document, so its changes may affect these levels.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
System security depends on algorithms and keys as well as the engineering and administration around them. The RFC says algorithms marked MUST or SHOULD were not known to be broken when it was written, but this may not remain true indefinitely.

The document expects future revisions as cryptographic knowledge changes. It requires no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Algorithm recommendations can become outdated as research changes. The RFC expects future revisions and notes that secure operation also depends on keys and system administration.

items.label: ENCR_DES, ENCR_BLOWFISH, ENCR_3IDEA and related older methods
items.desc: Implementations must not support these methods for IPsec.
